newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat police start crackdown on crime in Mostar.
newsitem.headline: Croat police start crackdown on crime in Mostar.

text.p: Croatian police have arrested a Bosnian Croat warlord and five other men in an apparent crackdown on organised crime in the divided town of Mostar, Western diplomats and state media said on Wednesday.

Mladen Naletilic, also known as Tuta, was arrested on Monday near the town of Split in southern Croatia and brought to a prison in Zagreb for questioning, the state news agency HINA quoted the Interior Ministry as saying.

Naletilic, often accused by international mediators of having connections with organised crime in Mostar, was arrested "on a well-founded suspicion that he was involved in committing a criminal act liable to official prosecution", the police told Hina without specifying the nature of the act.

A diplomat in Sarajevo who asked not to be named confirmed Naletilic was apprehended while another prominent warlord in Croat-held western Mostar, Vinko Martinovic known as "Stela", had escaped arrest.

"Croat police tried to arrest him but he escaped and he is on the run. A warrant has been issued for his arrest," the source told Reuters. It was not clear when or where Croat police had attempted to nab Martinovic.
The diplomat said there was a rumour the police may also have arrested about a dozen of Naletilic's men, but the report could not be confirmed.

In another indication that things may be changing in Mostar, HINA reported that Croat police there on Wednesday seized five men, all Croats, for armed robbery and issued arrest warrants for another three.

The arrests coincided with Western pressure on the Croatian government to bring into line ethnic Croats in Herzegovina, who oppose building joint political institutions with their nominal Moslem allies in the Bosnian Federation.
Another Western source told Reuters Croatian President Franjo Tudjman has probably been asked by senior diplomats this week "to remove once and for all" the gangsters in Mostar.
Croatia's state television, the mouthpiece for Tudjman and his ruling HDZ party, last week aired a commentary containing a the first veiled criticism of Croat mafia in Mostar in years.

"We may as well ask if the culprits are always on the Moslem side only, or if there is someone responsible (among Croats)," the commentary said, adding the crimes in Mostar may tarnish Croatia's reputation and damage its lucrative tourist industry.

International police investigators reported on Tuesday that Bosnian Croat police fired on unarmed Moslems without cause and behaved in a criminal manner in a February 10 incident in which a Moslem civilian was killed and some twenty wounded in Mostar.

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind asked on Wednesday that the culprits be brought to justice and urged the Croatian government to "use its influence with the Croat authorities in Mostar to ensure acceptance of the report".

Naletilic and Martinovic have frequently been accused by Western mediators of being at the centre of a powerful mafia cartel that runs western Mostar and opposes international efforts to build a stable peace in the region.
During the Bosnian war Naletilic commanded a notorious paramilitary unit of former convicts which operated in the Mostar area as part of the Bosnian Croat HVO militia.
Paramilitary units connected with mafia are held largely responsible for lawlessness in the western half of the sharply divided town, especially for the continuous evictions of Moslem inhabitants.
